title: Jukai Retreat
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett emphasizes that true progress in Zen practice involves embracing imperfection, being willing to confront challenges, and cultivating kindness, wisdom, and gentleness. This is reflected in the ordination ceremony, which is not about achieving perfection but rather about receiving Buddhist training and empowerment as a lifelong commitment to the spiritual path. By embracing this approach, individuals can deepen their understanding of themselves and the world around them, finding comfort and guidance in the present moment despite life's challenges.

sentences.text: *Good morning.
A few lines from Rilke.
You must not understand this life.
Then every day will be a feast.
Simply let every day be like a child who, passing by, receives many flowers from the wind.
She doesn't collect or save them.
That doesn't even occur to her.
They are lost from her hair where they were so happily arranged, and in the sweet years of her youth she reaches out to embrace the new.*
*You must not understand this life.
Then every day will be a feast.
Simply let every day be like a child who, passing by, receives many flowers from the wind.
She doesn't collect or save them.
That doesn't even occur to her.
They are lost from her hair where they were so happily arranged, and in the sweet years of her youth she reaches out to embrace the new.*
So I thought I'd share a few words about the ceremony we're going to do this afternoon.
If it isn't feeling so relevant to you, it's okay.
Just breathe.
The ceremony we're doing this afternoon for Jeffrey and Bob and Georgia is actually a kind of ordination ceremony, and yet the three of them aren't becoming ordained in the usual sense of that word.
So it's like an ordination for lay people.
When I started in Zen we usually called this ceremony lay ordination, which is wonderfully oxymoronic and appropriate.
So maybe the ceremony doesn't really fit our categories so well.
Now when we talk about it we usually focus on the fact that in the center of all Zen ordinations, priest or lay, are the precepts and the receiving of precepts.
So we usually say Jukai to signify this ceremony.
Ju just means receive and kai just means precepts.
So: receiving precepts.
All ordination ceremonies in Zen are empowerments around precepts practice.
Precepts practice, we hope, will in the end support us in being kinder, more helpful to all beings, wiser, gentler.
And so Buddhism as a religion seems to be designed from the inside out to be a force for good, and one hopes all religious practice has that design.
We don't like to talk about progress in Zen practice too much, because we get so quickly involved in trying to acquire something we don't have, and we think about progress.
And yet for sure there is change and progress, otherwise why would we do all this?
As we progress in the Dharma there is a kind of spiritual power, if you want to call it that, that seems to gather in you or around you or through you.
Sometimes this expresses in different ways, sometimes as a kind of attraction or a kind of charisma.
We really want to hang around with people who have been practicing for a long time, with a good feeling, because there's a real feeling to being with them, don't you think?
It's hard to put your finger on it but it's there.
Maybe stability, maybe some kind of charm or a sense of passion, devotion, some kind of wisdom maybe.

Of course as we get to know our wise teachers and senior practitioners, we remember from time to time that they're ordinary confused humans too, and sometimes that's a little bit of a fall from grace.
So it's both ordinary and special.

And as we progress through these different formal stages of practice, first we have this ceremony, Jukai, and maybe some people go on to additional ceremonies: lay entrustment, novice priest ordination, the empowerment of being Shuso, head student in a practice period, Dharma transmission, Dharma heritage ceremony.
So we have many empowerments and special ceremonies that seem to revolve around some people in the middle of the circle.
Of course they're created by the whole circle.
You could never do this without the rest of the sangha and lineage.
But what's interesting about every one of these ceremonies is that every one of them has at its core these same precepts, the 16 bodhisattva precepts.
If we were designing it we would have advanced precepts for the later stages, right?
We'd have a way of checking off our progress, but they didn't think about it that way.
So today Jeffrey, Bob, and Georgia will receive these 16 bodhisattva precepts very specifically, one at a time, with magical signals to say that they've really done this.
But what's interesting about precepts is all the other practices of Zen, of Mahayana Buddhism, of old Buddhism.
One of the lists we've studied a bunch lately, the list of six paramita practices, seems relevant, because one of those six, shila paramita, means ethical conduct, means precepts.
So all the precepts are inside that perfect practice, but we know that we can't do these practices outside of the support, the context, of all the other practices.

So our precepts practice, our expression of perfection of ethical conduct, can't be done without generosity, without patience, without devotion and energy, without stabilizing the mind, and without really exploring deeply prajnaparamita, the discerning wisdom of the buddhas.

We really need prajnaparamita to help us start to understand and to feel into when we're actually being of real benefit, or when we just think we're being helpful and actually it's in some way for our own self.
And even if it is, that's okay.
We learn as much or maybe more from our contraction and our suffering and our confusion as we do from when we feel the wonderful settled feeling of being in alignment with dharma and the universe.
As a sangha we're also trying to clarify our shared commitment in sangha life to living a way together that's clear, that's wise and resilient.
We're trying to clarify how the precepts play out in sangha life, and also what to do when they're not playing out so well and somebody gets hurt, because we know somebody's going to get hurt.
Somebody is hurt already for sure, and there's also the hurt of being the one who has in some way done the hurting.
So we've been trying to create a process.

We started with this sort of conventional idea of conflict resolution, we threw that out, and we're trying to do something bigger than that, because that's how we roll around here I guess, which makes it hard to do, but that's okay.

What's beautiful here is that by taking this public commitment these three worthy students are really affirming their willingness to engage so fully in this practice, in this process of sangha life and practice, 100 percent, 110 percent, who knows how much percent.
When I was sitting down to write the talk I ran into a quote blipped into my inbox about conflict and trouble in sangha life, from a Zen teacher in LA I think, Diane Musho Hamilton.
Here's what she wrote:
*Learning how to negotiate conflict demands that we become more present, more fearless.
We may need to relinquish the hopeful image of ourselves as remaining serene.
Three people who are recently in tears sewing their rakusu are all laughing.
We may have to let go of being like sitting buddhas carved from wood or stone.
We have to expect our composure to be compromised as we learn about the possibilities and creative solutions of working directly with the conflict in our relationships.
Even and maybe especially when things don't turn out the way we want, our engagement with discord refines and teaches us and alters our life's course.*
So I thought, that's good.
Our document's going to get longer and longer, but maybe we should stick that on there.
It's really good.
Unless we think we're just going to clean things up if we learn how to practice the precepts or become a Buddhist or something.
So that's our commitment as students of precepts: to be more present, more willing, more fearless, and more willing to fall apart.
Our ceremony this afternoon is actually a combination of two different Japanese Zen ceremonies.
I want to delve a little bit into the technicalities here just so we know.
Jukai, the part where we vow to follow the precepts, is one part of the ceremony, the first part, but most of the ceremony is actually another ceremony called Zaikei Tokudo.
That's the part where we receive a new name, new clothing, and a lineage, entry into the family, into the lineage.
In Zaikei Tokudo we become Buddhists in a way, in that we join Buddha's family.
Of course Buddha didn't have the idea of that word Buddhist, so I never know.
People say, what does it take to be a Buddhist?
I don't really know.
Are we Buddhists?
Anyway, of course we wouldn't enter into Buddha's family unless we're willing to really understand and abide by the family rules of the Buddhist house.
So Jukai and Zaikei Tokudo go together well, but they're often done separately in Japan apparently.
Zaikei means staying home, very literal: two characters, one means stay, one means home.
Tokudo means attain the way, so stay home, attain the way.
Ordination is the gloss they gave to Tokudo, attain the way.
I don't know if they have a word exactly that means ordination, like in English.
So it's kind of an ordination.
And then the priest ordination is Shukkei Tokudo.
There's the same kei, home, except shu was leaving home.
So Shukkei Tokudo was leaving home, attaining the way.

That's really a reference to the original monastic ideal of leaving your home, letting go of your birth family and your possessions and your plan and your career and all that, and just living like a mendicant monk or nun.
But in practice, in our actual modern societies, Asian and Western, it's all more mixed up.

Young priests in Japanese temple families receive Shukkei Tokudo probably in their late teens, which means home-leaving ordination, the purpose of which is that they can stay home and live in the temple and work there the rest of their lives.

So they enact the ritual of home leaving by going off to a training monastery for a couple of years, around age 20 or so. [unclear: "Ahiji"] that we visited in Japan is one of the big training monasteries, and even so it's not that big.
There are like a hundred monks there.
I don't know how many hundreds of thousands of people are in seminaries everywhere else, but it's a small movement.
Then they go back home and complete the ordination cycle, often with their father, and they often are young men.
It's a male-dominated system in Japan.
In Korea, I'm happy to find out, the nuns have a much closer equality to the male monastics.
I don't know as much about their system.
So to do a version of Tokudo, to do a kind of ordination for lay people, was like a super genius innovation of Soto Zen in the 13th and 14th centuries.
Because this way a priest could empower and support ordinary people, farming people in a village somewhere, with ordination, with entry into something big and mysterious and vast.
Because in most cultures throughout the world, the clergy are the educated elite, right?
And the non-educated, non-elite are held down.
So Soto Zen somehow had this impulse to be a little more inclusive, and it was like the secret to their success.
My understanding is that in the state-sponsored Zen of the capital, this would be unheard of.
They did have a ceremony like the Jukai we do, but it was mostly done to acknowledge donors, important people, like you would think.
And if you're really important, you would get a posthumous ordination when you die, ordain your body so you can have a monk's funeral.
So ordaining lay people is a powerful idea, even if it's not exactly ordination.

The other power of it was that many of these folks in villages in feudal Japan were seeing their names written down for the first time in their lives, on the documents that they receive in the ceremony, the documents you'll receive in the ceremony today, same documents.
So very powerful, in some ways, I'm sure very generous and inclusive, and in other ways another way to maintain power.
It's always a mix.
So we're going to receive these documents today, lineage documents.
The other thing that the three ordinees receive today, this bib-like garment called rakusu, was probably invented in China.
We don't really know.
Apparently the archaeological evidence is not good.
It was probably invented in China in the eighth century as a response to intense persecution of Buddhism, which was at that point a foreign religion.
It was pretty intense actually, apparently: soldiers everywhere destroying temples and killing or defrocking clergy.
And so the theory is that the clergy invented a kind of secret robe that they could wear underneath their farmer clothes or whatever they had to be after that.
The wearing of this garment died out in China sometime, but continues very strongly in Japan and Korea.

Now the rakusu is worn by lay people who have gone through this ceremony we'll do this afternoon, whenever they practice, as a reminder of that part of their lives, that family that they're a member of.
It's also worn by the priest-ordained clergy in semi-formal situations.
Like I wore mine to Dharma meetings, sangha meetings and stuff.
I wore it when I visited a patient at the hospice the other day.
I think it would have been unwieldy to wear the full robe.
The rakusu is actually a sort of miniature version of the full robe worn by Buddhist clergy in all Buddhist cultures.
This outer brown robe here is just a great big rectangle wrapped around the body.
In original Buddhism in India, and which persists pretty consistently through into Burma, Thailand, Sri Lanka, the rest of the clothing was also prescribed and is quite different from these robes.
The robes that were under the outer robe, the okesa it's called, are actually an adaptation of Chinese clerical robes.
Because in China they had a whole system of robes and special hats to show your status.
So we have all this history going on here.
It's interesting.
The pattern of the pieces that are sewn together on this robe, or in the center frame of the rakusu, is supposed to be from the Buddha going on a walk one day, looking across at some rice fields.
That's the way it's told in Asian Buddhism.
I'm not really sure that they had rice in the Ganges basin at that time, but some kind of fields.
And saying, well, look at that beautiful pattern, fields and paths.
Let's make our robes like that.
So we're wearing rice fields.
Our robes are both exotic religious garments, a long history from a whole other culture in a way, but also farms, also rooted in the earth and very simple.
Once it's all together it looks simple.
So you would think that everyone in the sangha who feels serious about our practice and sangha life should get going, right?
Should get out their needle and thread and start sewing and preparing for the ceremony.
If it's an important thing, why wouldn't you do it?
And we have a mind that wants to know what the next step is, right?
People are asking, what do I do next?
How do I do it right?
What's the next step?
How do we make progress?
Some of us may end up doing that.
That would be wonderful.
But I also hope plenty of us in our sangha family feel full permission not to do any of this stuff.
For some of us this overt engagement with the religiosity of Buddhism and these powerful archetypal symbols isn't right.
That's totally fine.
What a wonderful thing to be a serious student of Zen or of meditation, or maybe you just call it sitting.
What's exotic about sitting?
What do you do to really care for yourself?
I just sit around and I sit.
Very ordinary, right?
So what a wonderful thing to be engaged in Zen practice in a very ordinary way, without all this as well.
And we have that archetype in our Zen symbolic treasury as well.
What the great master Rinzai called, somewhat sexistly, the man of no rank.
The person, he said man apparently, but we'll say person, the person of no rank.
That's a deep ideal of our practice: to just blend in, to be unnoticed, to be a quiet source of peace and stability.
And of course, religion is always ironical a little bit.
So Rinzai, who invented that, was himself prominent clergy, abbot of a state-sponsored temple with a good salary.
But it's a great idea.
But if it does feel like something that's interesting to you, to us, to follow in the beautiful footsteps of these three worthies today, here are a few thoughts.
First, it's good if you've practiced in this style for at least several years, two or three at least.

Next, it's good to have conversations with one of our teachers, with me or one of the five others who have completed the Shuso training and are empowered to have private interviews, to talk about your interest in that and how it really feels.
None of us have exactly the psychic powers to look inside your head and see if that's right for you.
If we say we do, you know what to do.
But we can help you explore and listen carefully to the feeling of your aspiration.
Sometimes it's better to wait a little longer.
Sometimes, yeah, maybe it's not for you.
Should I do Jukai?
What do you think?
And really listen.
And then if a teacher agrees, great idea, and would like to support you in the process, then we study the precepts.
What's great about this, and it's pretty fluid, is that we can study the precepts and have that not result in these fancy ceremonies and clothes too.
It's always good to study the precepts.
So far the precept study has been a little bit ad hoc.
Once or twice we've had a class in precepts.
I've mostly been working with people individually, having five to ten dokusan meetings to reflect carefully on these 16 precepts.
I ask people to read commentaries.
We never get tired of Robert Aitken's Mind of Clover.
We'll read that over and over again until we all die.
There are many other commentaries that are very good, but mostly we use the comments and teachings of others as support to look at our own self, at our own heart, at our own life.
How do these precepts come alive in my life?
And it's been really beautiful meeting with these three as they explore that.
But maybe in the next year or so we'll have some kind of more regular study group around the precepts.

We could all study the precepts regularly, because it's also really wonderful to have conversations with friends, with peers, about your precepts practice, whether you're new to that idea or have been doing this for decades.
And somewhere in this process of precept study, one receives permission from the teacher to start sewing the rakusu.

Of course there you instantly realize you're going to need a lot of help, because it's a sort of arcane process to take a piece of fabric, mark it very precisely with millimeter tolerances into little rectangles, cut it into pieces and sew it back together again.
That's like the Zen story, it's probably a myth, of somebody during the work period at the monastery going along pulling weeds, and somebody behind them is sticking them back in the ground.
It's a little bit like that.
It's great Zen process.
With this time around, we all ended up in a bit of a crunch with the sewing one way or the other.
I'm looking forward to having more regular support with sewing teachers, but maybe it's inevitable that we have to hit some walls as we do this process.
When Chris Burkhart comes back she has the aspiration of regular sewing groups, and maybe we'll have that.
And out of necessity Kate here became a glorious sewing coach.
Can we say that?
Going to hang in there with people to the death.
Wonderful.
So I think even though we stumbled around a little bit, we collectively learned a little more about sewing this last year, which is really wonderful.
Because the stitching and piecing itself is a powerful Dharma practice.
It is not just a means to the end of having this thing that you have to get done in time for a special ceremony.
Every stitch is an exploration of what does this mean?
What is this?
What is this?
And with every stitch we say in Japanese, I take refuge in Buddha.
I take refuge in Buddha.
Every time we say it, it feels a little different, yeah?
A little different meaning every time.
*Namu Kie Butsu.
Namu Kie Butsu.*
Sometimes we forget for a while.
And this act of sewing and creating this spiritual symbol can do a lot to a person or with a person.
It really can work us psychologically, spiritually.
Our perfectionism is the first to fall.
You cannot make a precise hand-stitched garment like this the first time and have it not come out looking really wonky to the eyes of the perfectionist.
It looks very beautiful to some other eyes, but to the eyes of the perfectionist it's like, ah!
Should I rip that out?
And it works us in all other kinds of ways too, doing this process of sewing this garment as dharma practice, psychologically and spiritually.
It's really hard to know what's going on.
In the end, do we sew the rakusu?
Where's the rakusu sewing us?
It really surprises people, and it surprises me every time, to do this myself or see somebody go through it: wow, amazing.
Once the student has managed to finish sewing the rakusu, it's given to the teacher, who empowers it by writing the student's new name and some encouraging words on the back.
And it's given to the student in the ceremony.
So in a way you make it, but in a way you receive it and you didn't make it.
It's not yours exactly.
As it's purified and received in the ceremony, that's when it becomes fully a rakusu.
That moment when the teacher purifies it one last time in the incense and hands it to you and you take it in the hands: these are the hands of Buddha that receive it.
In that moment it's a rakusu.
Until then it's cloth.
And on the rakusu is written one's new name, and this is a powerful part of the process as well.

The teacher is trying to call on Buddha for help to come up with a name that will support the person, the practitioner, in really taking up their identity, their true identity, as a child of Buddha, as one who vows to live a life of precepts and service.

So I also want to mention where our local sanghas differ a little bit, which is in their understanding of what this means going forward in your relationship to the teacher or teachers you studied with in the preparation.
And actually, it's funny, I've spoken within the last couple of weeks with both a teacher to the south and a teacher to the north about this, so we've been comparing notes.
Jeff Kelly in Seattle, to the south, in his lineage they don't see jukai as particularly an important marker for formalizing the student-teacher relationship.
The focus is more on precepts practice, and of course you need a teacher, and a teacher you feel good about for sure, but it doesn't imply an ongoing commitment or relationship with that teacher.
It implies an ongoing relationship to practice and precepts in the lineage of Soto Zen he studied in.
Meanwhile Peter Levitt in the north, on Salt Spring Island, has the opposite idea, so it's great, there's diversity.

He feels it's a very serious commitment between him and the student, and his expectation is that if you receive precepts from him you'll stay in touch with him, speaking with him at least once a month, speaking to him about all major life decisions, listening, not obeying but listening to what he has to say, and staying in a real sense of strong contact and commitment with him.
I just didn't ask him for how long.
Maybe forever, I don't know.
That latter understanding is a little more how I understand priest ordination, and Peter's a lay teacher, so maybe he holds those two in a combined way.
The way that I feel we receive from Norman Fischer is somewhere in between.
To receive [unclear: "ryokasu"] and a name from a teacher, it's a warming of the relationship.
It's a deep and intimate thing to do together, and it's an expression of love.
I certainly would be happy if everyone that receives jukai from me keeps in touch and lets me know if they're upset with me, or something else is going on, or they're ready to stop practicing now.
But I don't really expect anything exactly.
It seems like one wouldn't want to receive jukai if one wasn't committed to practicing in this way for at least a number of years, but I don't see it as a lifetime commitment.
I see it as an expression of what we are now and where we are now, that has a lot of room for growth and change.
Maybe five years later you all become Catholics, I don't know.
Not likely.
Not that there's anything wrong with that.
And like I mentioned, I see the priest ordination as a little more of a lifetime commitment to this way of practice and the teacher you ordain with.
So that's a little bit what we're doing today and what's now a little more available to us as a community.
And of course we've had jukai for many years through Norman Fischer as our preceptor, and Norman Fischer happily remains alive and kicking, and Becky was at the Loon Lake sesshin this last week.
Says he's doing well.
Gave some beautiful talks on the merging of difference and unity, and I'll see him in December myself.

The other thing that I really appreciate about the style of practice we receive from Norman is that even though we really do honor the formalized depth of this (you cannot receive precepts from someone who is not himself or herself a preceptor, and to be a preceptor in our lineage you need to be ordained and have completed dharma transmission, and that's it), we can collaborate.
So I got to collaborate with Norman when I was not a preceptor and he was, in some of the jukai that we've had in our community, where we worked together on the name and the rakusu.

Something like that will happen here as well, with me or even a visiting priest as preceptor and some of our lay teachers as the primary supporter of the student, the one they did a lot of their precept study with.
So we can be fluid about it.
I think we can be fluid and we can honor the particulars of our tradition and not change them, even if it would be convenient to change them.
Let's end with one more poem, my all-time favorite, which I probably quote too often.
*You do not have to be good.
You do not have to walk on your knees for a hundred miles through the desert repenting.
You only have to let the soft animal of your body love what it loves.
Tell me about despair.
Yours, and I will tell you mine.
Meanwhile the world goes on.
Meanwhile the sun and the clear pebbles of the rain are moving across the landscapes, over the prairies and the deep trees, the mountains and the rivers.
Meanwhile the wild geese, high in the clean blue air, are heading home again.
Whoever you are, no matter how lonely, the world offers itself to your imagination, calls to you like the wild geese, harsh and exciting, over and over announcing your place in the family of things.*
This is Mary Oliver, of course: "Wild Geese."
*You do not have to be good.
You do not have to walk on your knees for a hundred miles through the desert repenting.
You only have to let the soft animal of your body love what it loves.
Tell me about despair.
Yours, and I will tell you mine.
Meanwhile the world goes on.
Meanwhile the sun and the clear pebbles of the rain are moving across the landscapes, over the prairies and the deep trees, the mountains and the river.
Meanwhile the wild geese, high in the clean blue air, are heading home again.
Whoever you are, no matter how lonely, the world offers itself to your imagination, calls to you like the wild geese, harsh and exciting, over and over announcing your place in the family of things.*
